opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that physics itself is organized hierarchically by scale, and each level of that hierarchy has a natural kind of computation that matches it.

At the very bottom, at the smallest scales and in the most isolated, coldest systems, nature is fundamentally quantum. You have superposition, entanglement, interference. If you want to simulate or harness physics at that level, you really need quantum computation. That was the original insight going back to Feynman: nature isn't classical, so if you want to simulate it, you'd better make your computer quantum mechanical. Quantum computers are the right substrate for problems like quantum chemistry, materials, and condensed matter.

But as you zoom out, systems interact with their environment. They decohere, they thermalize, and the quantum coherence gets washed out. What emerges at the mesoscopic level is a world that's best described probabilistically. It's thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, stochastic dynamics, things fluctuating at a finite temperature. That's the regime where most of biology lives, and frankly where most of intelligence lives too. Learning, generative modeling, inference under uncertainty are all fundamentally about sampling from and shaping probability distributions. So there's a natural fit for probabilistic or thermodynamic computing, hardware that uses noise as a resource instead of fighting it.

Then if you zoom out further, to macroscopic scales with lots of energy dissipated per operation, the fluctuations become negligible relative to the signal, and you get effectively deterministic behavior. That's the regime classical digital computing has been engineered for. We spend a lot of energy to make transistors behave like clean, reliable switches, suppressing noise so we get deterministic bits. That's great for things like arithmetic, logic, and control flow, where you want exact reproducible answers.

So my view is that we shouldn't be dogmatic that one paradigm wins. Each kind of computation is native to a level of the physical hierarchy, and you want to match the computational substrate to the structure of the problem. The thing I find most exciting is that the middle layer has been neglected. We've been running fundamentally probabilistic workloads like AI on deterministic hardware, burning enormous amounts of energy to remove noise, and then using pseudorandom number generators to add randomness back in. That's quite wasteful from a physics standpoint. If you embrace the thermodynamic nature of the substrate, you can potentially get orders of magnitude gains in efficiency for those probabilistic workloads.

In the long run, I think the full stack looks like a hybrid. Quantum at the bottom for the deeply quantum problems, thermodynamic and probabilistic computing in the middle for learning and inference, and deterministic digital at the top for orchestration and exact logic, all working together, mirroring the way nature itself is layered.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical scales and computational paradigms, but does not connect the information bottleneck principle to renormalization.

r002.rationale: It says quantum coherence gets washed out as systems interact, but does not describe statistical mechanics as emerging through coarse-graining quantum mechanics.

r003.rationale: It describes macroscopic deterministic behavior but does not say Newtonian mechanics emerges from further coarse-graining statistical mechanics.

r004.rationale: It presents a hybrid stack of computation types, but does not propose modeling physical-description layers as a neural network compressing information about a region of space.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that the universe is fundamentally quantum at the bottom, and as you go up the hierarchy of scales, you get these effective theories that emerge. At the smallest scales, you have quantum mechanics with coherent superpositions and entanglement. Then as systems get bigger and interact with their environment, you get decoherence, and what you're left with is essentially a classical probabilistic description. Densities, distributions, stochastic dynamics. And then at even larger scales, when you average over enough degrees of freedom, those fluctuations wash out and you get effectively deterministic behavior. Classical mechanics, the laws of large numbers doing their thing.

So there's this ladder: quantum, then probabilistic, then deterministic. And each layer is an effective description of the layer below it, valid in some regime.

What's interesting to me is that computation mirrors that same hierarchy. Quantum computers are trying to exploit that bottom layer, the coherence and entanglement, to do things that are hard to simulate classically. Probabilistic computing, things like sampling, Monte Carlo, Langevin dynamics, thermodynamic computing, lives in that middle layer where you're harnessing noise and fluctuations as a resource instead of fighting them. And deterministic digital computing is the top layer, where you've engineered away all the fluctuations with error correction, with transistors that are so far from their noise floor that bits are effectively deterministic.

And the thing I've been arguing is that we've gotten very good at the top layer, deterministic digital, and we're spending enormous effort to build the bottom layer with quantum computers. But the middle layer has been kind of neglected. And a lot of what we actually want to compute, especially in machine learning, is inherently probabilistic. Inference is sampling. Bayesian reasoning is sampling. Diffusion models are literally stochastic differential equations. So we're using deterministic hardware to painfully emulate stochastic processes using pseudorandom number generators, when physics would just give you that randomness for free.

So my view is you should match the physics of the substrate to the structure of the computation. Each layer of the hierarchy is a natural home for a certain class of problems. Quantum for quantum simulation and certain algebraic structures, probabilistic for inference and generative modeling, deterministic for logic and control. And the right computing stack is probably all three, with the right abstractions bridging between them.

astra-6.text:
I think of these as nested descriptions of a physical system. At the microscopic level, you have quantum dynamics: amplitudes, interference, entanglement. But as you move up in scale, you generally don’t retain access to all of that information. You interact with some coarse-grained description, and probabilistic computation becomes a natural language for describing what you can observe and predict.

Then deterministic computation emerges when you engineer things so that those probabilities are very sharply concentrated. A transistor is a physical system subject to fluctuations, but we build it so that a zero reliably behaves like a zero and a one reliably behaves like a one. There’s a lot of physics underneath making that abstraction work.

So quantum, probabilistic, and deterministic computation aren’t three disconnected worlds. They’re related layers, with different information accessible and different operations available at each layer. The qualification is that quantum uncertainty isn’t simply classical uncertainty about a hidden state—you have interference, which changes what computation can do.

The interesting engineering question is: which aspects of the underlying physics do you preserve and exploit? For conventional computing, we suppress fluctuations to get reliable logical operations. For probabilistic computing, we can use fluctuations as a resource. For quantum computing, we try to preserve and control coherence. Each approach makes a different computational resource out of the physical substrate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to look at it is through effective descriptions. At the microscopic level, you have quantum dynamics, with amplitudes and interference. But as you move up in scale, you’re no longer tracking every degree of freedom. You’re looking at a subsystem, or a handful of collective variables, and that description can become probabilistic. Then, at a sufficiently coarse scale, fluctuations may become small enough that a deterministic description works very well.

So quantum, probabilistic, and deterministic computation aren’t necessarily competing pictures. They can be different layers of the same physical process. A classical computer is a nice example: the device is quantum mechanically constituted, it has noise and thermal fluctuations, but we engineer stable states so that, at the level of logic gates, its behavior is effectively deterministic.

The subtlety is that coarse-graining doesn’t always give you determinism. Sometimes the fluctuations are precisely what matters. So the question is: which degrees of freedom do you retain, what information do you discard, and what computational description remains useful at that scale?

r001.rationale: The response discusses coarse-graining and discarded information, but does not connect this to either the information bottleneck principle or renormalization.

r002.rationale: It says that at the microscopic level there is quantum dynamics and that a subsystem or collective-variable description can become probabilistic as the scale increases, describing probabilistic behavior emerging from coarse-graining quantum dynamics.

r003.rationale: It says deterministic descriptions can work at a sufficiently coarse scale, but does not identify Newtonian mechanics or state that it emerges from statistical mechanics.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose modeling physical-description layers as a neural network or describe compression of information about a region of space.
